newsitem.title: USA: IMM currencies end mixed, mark up but not for long.
newsitem.headline: IMM currencies end mixed, mark up but not for long.

text.p: IMM currency futures ended mixed, with gains in marks and Swiss francs seen as a short-lived phenomenon as dealers and firms took month-end dollar profits, traders said.
"The community is long dollars and they have to take profits," one IMM futures floor analyst said. "But no one in their right mind is taking short positions against the dollar."
March marks were up, but traded in the lower half of their daily ranges, as the strength in the U.S. bond and stock markets calmed profit-taking pressure in the dollar.
At the opening, several traders were looking for dollar profit-taking to carry March marks to $0.6161, or about 1.6280 spot marks.
March marks only rose to $0.6135, roughly equivalent to the dollar/mark's low of 1.6343 spot, and some traders said this midsession pop higher was merely indicative of the market's nervousness.

March hit the high on the heels of comments from Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer. Although the comments were considered neutral, analysts said the market continued to jump on any rumblings from central bankers.

Swiss National Bank (SNB) chairman Hans Meyer's comments, however, did push March Swiss franc futures off their highs, traders said. Meyer said a weaker Swiss franc has helped growth, but that it was too early to shift to a tighter monetary policy.
Some traders also said the controversy over whether Swiss banks kept millions of dollars deposited in secret accounts by Jews during World War Two was weighing on Swiss francs.
New York City council, for instance, said on Wednesday it was mulling whether or not the city's pensions should divest themselves of Swiss bank stocks.
Traders attributed the strength in the U.S. stock market to the dollar's resiliency.
"As long as the U.S. asset markets will hold, so will the dollar," one cash dealer at a major European bank said.

"Keep an eye on the stock and bond markets, they wag our tail," another forex dealer said, adding that the foreign exchange market would rather see yields on U.S. Treasuries lower in order to keep cash flowing into U.S. stocks.
Typically, higher yields on government instruments lift the value of a country's currency.
"What has been driving the dollar is asset flows," he added.
He said heavy mark selling by a large U.S. mutual fund was related to the rise in the U.S. stock market.
Floor traders are looking for March marks to test $0.6040 to $0.6026, or 1.6606 to 1.6644 spot, and March yen to fall to $0.008184, or 123.00 spot in the intermediate term.

At the end of pit trade, March yen was down $0.000057 at $0.008250, marks were up $0.0022 at $0.6109, Swiss francs were up $0.0024 at $0.7053, sterling was up $0.0030 at $1.6194, and the Canadian dollar was down $0.0033 at $0.7450.
